paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using observations collected under another policy. This paper addresses the choice of estimator for that evaluation. Rather than committing to one estimator in advance, the authors develop a generic method that uses the available data to make the selection. The contribution therefore concerns how to choose an evaluation method, rather than introducing only a single fixed estimator.

The central theoretical result compares the selection procedure with an oracle estimator: a reference representing the ideal estimator choice in the comparison. The authors establish that their method is competitive with that oracle up to a constant factor. This is a qualified performance guarantee, rather than a claim that the selected estimator always exactly matches the oracle.

The paper examines the approach through detailed studies in contextual bandits and reinforcement learning. These two settings demonstrate its applicability across different policy evaluation problems. Comprehensive experiments also compare it with related approaches, with favorable results in both case studies. Together, the theory and experiments support using data-driven selection as a practical component of off-policy evaluation.
icml-2020-adaptive-estimator-selection-f.tldr: A data-driven estimator selection method offers an oracle-relative performance guarantee and favorable results in bandit and reinforcement learning policy evaluation.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks learn by comparing a generated distribution with the data distribution through a discriminator. The paper starts from a tradeoff between two families of these models. Wasserstein GANs have strong empirical performance, while f-GANs provide estimates of the ratio between model and data densities. Those ratios are useful beyond generation, including in inverse reinforcement learning.

The authors introduce a training objective that also optimizes importance weights assigned to generated samples. These weights become part of the optimization rather than leaving the objective fixed in its original form. By changing the constraints on which weights are permitted, the approach produces a family of objectives that includes both the original f-GAN and Wasserstein GAN objectives.

This construction connects the two families within a common framework and supports extensions beyond either original objective. The authors report that a natural extension outperforms Wasserstein GANs while retaining density-ratio estimation. Experiments cover distribution modeling, density-ratio estimation, and image generation. The stated benefit is therefore both a unifying formulation and an empirically successful way to combine useful capabilities.
icml-2020-bridging-the-gap-between-f-gan.tldr: Optimizing weights on generated samples connects f-GAN and Wasserstein GAN objectives while supporting strong generation and density-ratio estimation.

paragraphs: Adversarial training usually prepares a classifier for a specified kind and size of input perturbation. Its protection often transfers poorly to other attacks. This paper proposes confidence-calibrated adversarial training, or CCAT, which encourages low-confidence predictions on adversarial examples. The system can then reject inputs whose confidence falls below a threshold.

Rejection is central to the reported generalization of robustness. A model trained with one threat model can avoid confidently accepting some attacks outside that model. Using training attacks constrained by the L-infinity norm, the authors report improved robustness to larger perturbations of that type, several other norm-based attacks, adversarial frames, distal adversarial examples, and corrupted inputs. They also report better clean accuracy than adversarial training.

The evaluation explicitly challenges the confidence mechanism. The authors develop white-box and black-box attacks that seek high-confidence predictions, using seven attacks per threat model with up to fifty restarts and five thousand iterations. They report the worst robust test error across attacks under their confidence-thresholded evaluation. The findings support broader robustness when low-confidence rejection is allowed, rather than guaranteed correct classification of every attacked input.
icml-2020-confidence-calibrated-adversar.tldr: Training models to express low confidence on adversarial inputs improves robustness to unseen attacks when uncertain predictions can be rejected.

paragraphs: Approximate Q-learning can suffer from delusional bias, an error connected to training targets that are inconsistent with the greedy policies the model can represent. The paper focuses on making those targets jointly compatible with the available policy class. Earlier methods explicitly addressing this problem required comprehensive search with tabular value estimates, motivating approaches suitable for learned Q-approximators.

The authors introduce a simple penalty that encourages consistency among Q-learning labels across training batches. Considering batches together matters because the desired compatibility concerns the collection of labels, rather than each label in isolation. This gives training a mechanism for discouraging combinations of targets that do not fit the expressible policy class.

A second contribution is a search framework that generates and tracks multiple Q-approximators. Keeping multiple candidates helps mitigate the consequences of committing implicitly to a policy too early. Experiments on a variety of Atari games show that these methods can improve Q-learning performance, with dramatic improvements in some cases. The results support consistency constraints and alternative candidates as ways to reduce delusional bias, without claiming that they eliminate it.
icml-2020-conqur-mitigating-delusional-b.tldr: ConQUR reduces delusional bias by encouraging compatible Q-learning targets and tracking alternative Q-approximators, improving performance on several Atari games.

paragraphs: This paper studies off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits: estimating a policy's performance from data collected under another policy. Its starting point is the doubly robust estimator, which has an asymptotic optimality property. The authors focus on finite datasets, where an estimator's behavior depends on the balance between systematic error, or bias, and variability across samples.

Their method shrinks importance weights by optimizing an upper bound on mean squared error. This makes weight adjustment part of a stated optimization problem. The resulting tradeoff permits some bias in exchange for reduced variance, improving finite-sample behavior. The framework produces a weight-clipping estimator, a new weight-shrinkage estimator, and a shrinkage-based estimator for combinatorial action sets.

The combinatorial extension broadens the framework beyond the standard bandit setting to problems with structured collections of possible actions. Extensive experiments examine both standard and combinatorial benchmarks. The authors find that their estimators adapt well and typically outperform state-of-the-art methods. The claim is an empirical tendency across the evaluated problems, supported by a framework designed around finite-sample error rather than asymptotic optimality alone.
icml-2020-doubly-robust-off-policy-evalu.tldr: Optimizing shrinkage of importance weights improves the finite-sample bias–variance tradeoff in doubly robust policy evaluation.

paragraphs: Autonomous racing makes the tension between safety and performance especially visible: excessive caution can undermine competitive performance, while other vehicles introduce uncertainty. FormulaZero addresses this setting through both preparation before deployment and adaptation during operation. The aim is to provide realistic behavioral variety among opponents and a robust way to respond when their behavior remains uncertain.

For preparation, the authors develop a self-play method based on replica-exchange Markov chain Monte Carlo. It generates a diverse, realistic population of opponents. For online adaptation, they introduce a distributionally robust bandit optimization procedure. This procedure adjusts risk aversion in relation to uncertainty in the system's beliefs about opponent behavior, connecting the treatment of risk to the information currently available.

The paper also rigorously quantifies performance and robustness tradeoffs when these computations are approximated for real-time motion planning. That analysis connects the proposed optimization methods to the need to make decisions quickly. Experiments demonstrate the approach on autonomous vehicles reaching scaled speeds comparable to Formula One racecars. These demonstrations support its use in demanding racing conditions without establishing universal safety.
icml-2020-formulazero-distributionally-r.tldr: FormulaZero combines diverse self-play opponents with uncertainty-sensitive risk adaptation for autonomous racing.

paragraphs: The paper examines momentum-based optimization when gradient noise has heavy tails, meaning unusually large disturbances can be consequential. Its main object is underdamped Langevin dynamics, a continuous-time variant of stochastic gradient descent with momentum. The authors investigate the distribution this process approaches over time in a setting relevant to non-convex learning.

Their theoretical and empirical argument is that heavy-tailed perturbations can introduce a persistent mismatch: the optima of the stationary distribution may differ from the optima of the cost function. Small step sizes do not necessarily remove this bias. The proposed remedy, fractional underdamped Langevin dynamics, is proved to target a Gibbs distribution whose optima match those of the original cost.

This guarantee concerns the target distribution, rather than asserting that every optimization run finds an optimum. The authors also examine an Euler discretization of their dynamics and identify algorithmic similarities with natural gradient methods and gradient clipping. These connections offer a perspective on how such techniques relate to heavy-tailed noise. Experiments on a synthetic model and neural networks support the theoretical analysis.
icml-2020-fractional-underdamped-langevi.tldr: Fractional underdamped Langevin dynamics corrects a possible heavy-tail-induced mismatch between an optimization process's stationary distribution and its cost function.

paragraphs: Generative Teaching Networks learn to produce training material that helps another network learn quickly. A learner trains on generated data or environments for a few stochastic gradient steps and is then evaluated on a target task. The teaching network is updated by differentiating through that learning process, so its output is shaped by the learner's resulting performance.

The central idea is to optimize the teaching process itself. Generated examples are useful insofar as they help a freshly initialized learner improve after a short training period. The formulation is theoretically applicable to supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, but the paper's experiments examine only supervised learning. Those experiments show that the method can substantially accelerate learning.

The authors apply this capability to evaluating candidate networks during neural architecture search. Holding the search proposal mechanism fixed, GTN-NAS finds higher-performing architectures and improves the reported state of the art. It is also competitive with leading approaches that use far less computation than typical search methods. The demonstrated contribution is accelerated supervised learning and architecture evaluation; broader self-generated learning environments remain a proposed direction.
icml-2020-generative-teaching-networks-a.tldr: Generative Teaching Networks learn synthetic training material through learner performance, accelerating supervised learning and neural architecture evaluation.

paragraphs: HyperCloud generates three-dimensional shapes through a network that produces the weights of another network. The second, or target, network transforms points sampled uniformly from a unit ball into points belonging to a shape. Generating a point cloud therefore means sampling input points and applying the shape-specific transformation one point at a time.

The hypernetwork uses an autoencoder architecture trained to reconstruct realistic shapes. Its output is a set of target-network weights, which the authors interpret as a parameterization of the object's surface. This allows the method to learn both an object representation and a representation of its three-dimensional surfaces, rather than returning only a conventional point-cloud representation.

The distinction matters because the learned object is associated with a transformation that can generate its geometry through sampling. The architecture also permits generative construction of mesh-based object representations. The authors report point-cloud quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The stated contribution combines competitive point generation with a surface-oriented representation that also supports meshes, rather than claiming an across-the-board improvement in point-cloud quality.
icml-2020-hypernetwork-approach-to-gener.tldr: HyperCloud generates shape-specific network weights that map sampled points into 3D objects and support both point-cloud and mesh representations.

paragraphs: Decentralized optimization distributes learning across nodes, making both local data access and communication important costs. This paper studies certain smooth, non-convex problems with m nodes and n samples at each node. Its goal is to reduce the sample requirements while keeping communication efficient, instead of considering only one of those resources.

The proposed D-GET algorithm combines gradient estimation with gradient tracking. Each node estimates its local gradient using a subset of local samples. Tracking then uses those local estimates to follow the global full gradient. The contribution is the joint use of these two mechanisms within a decentralized stochastic algorithm.

For a deterministic finite-sum problem, the authors establish sample complexity O(m√n/ε) and communication complexity O(1/ε) for the stated ε-stationarity criterion. Compared with the cited O(mn/ε) sample bound, this improves dependence on local dataset size while retaining the same communication order. For online problems, they obtain O(m/ε^(3/2)) sample complexity and O(1/ε) communication complexity. These are guarantees for reaching the specified stationary solution, rather than guarantees of finding a global optimum.
icml-2020-improving-the-sample-and-commu.tldr: D-GET combines local gradient estimation and global gradient tracking to improve sample complexity while maintaining efficient decentralized communication.

paragraphs: Connected devices produce telemetry with many measurements and multiple normal operating modes, such as occupied and vacant conditions. This paper proposes an unsupervised method for detecting departures from those modes. It creates artificial negative samples from observed positive samples, then trains a classifier to distinguish the two groups. The resulting classification problem provides a route to anomaly detection.

The authors use the concentration phenomenon to explain why this construction should produce useful boundaries between normal and anomalous regions. They also apply Integrated Gradients to attribute an anomalous state to particular measurement dimensions. This adds an explanatory component: the detector can identify which parts of the state vector contribute to its assessment.

Experiments with random forests and neural networks show significantly higher AUC scores than state-of-the-art approaches on benchmark datasets and real climate-control telemetry. The paper also reports large-scale deployment of neural-network classifiers for real-time failure prediction across more than fifteen thousand climate-control and power-meter devices in 145 office buildings. The evidence therefore spans benchmark discrimination, multidimensional operating data, and an operational deployment.
icml-2020-interpretable-multidimensional.tldr: Classifying observed telemetry against generated negative samples enables scalable anomaly detection with measurement-level explanations and demonstrated device deployment.

paragraphs: The paper aims to learn discrete, structured representations from unlabeled data. Its objective is to maximize mutual information between a structured latent variable and a target variable, encouraging the representation to preserve information about that target. Direct calculation of mutual information is intractable in the setting the authors consider, so the central challenge is making this learning objective usable.

The authors introduce an adversarial objective that permits tractable estimation of mutual information, assuming cross entropy can be calculated. That assumption is the stated computational requirement for their general formulation. They then build a concrete model using Markov distributions over binary encodings, giving the discrete representations an explicit probabilistic structure.

The paper also reports important and unexpected practical findings concerning choices such as variational priors. In document hashing, the resulting model outperforms the compared leading baselines based on discrete and vector-quantized variational autoencoders. It also produces highly compressed, interpretable representations. The contribution joins a tractable information-based learning objective with an application showing that structured binary representations can be both compact and useful.
icml-2020-learning-discrete-structured-r.tldr: An adversarial mutual-information objective learns compact structured binary representations and improves document hashing over the compared autoencoder baselines.

paragraphs: This paper uses a mathematical connection between neural networks and tropical algebra to reduce the size of trained multiclass classifiers. The connection applies to networks with piecewise-linear activations, whose outputs can be described using tropical polynomials in the max-plus semiring. That description provides an alternative mathematical form in which to study network simplification.

The authors develop methods based on approximate division of those polynomials. The division procedure relies on approximating associated geometric objects called Newton polytopes. By working through this algebraic and geometric representation, the methods seek smaller networks for multiclass classification. The paper contributes both proposed reduction procedures and theoretical analysis of them.

Experiments evaluate the approach on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. The authors report significant reductions in network size while preserving adequate performance. This supports the usefulness of the tropical-algebra connection for compression in the evaluated settings. The stated outcome is a favorable reduction with acceptable retained performance, rather than exact preservation of every prediction or a claim that compression causes no loss of accuracy.
icml-2020-multiclass-neural-network-mini.tldr: Approximating tropical-polynomial geometry reduces multiclass network size while retaining adequate performance on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST.

paragraphs: This paper revisits whether noise from minibatch stochastic gradient descent can improve performance on unseen data. A competing explanation is that large-batch methods only appear worse because their hyperparameters are poorly tuned or their computation budgets are insufficient. The authors address that dispute through carefully designed experiments and rigorous hyperparameter sweeps across several popular models.

They find that small or moderately large batches can substantially outperform very large batches on the test set. This occurs even when training uses the same number of iterations and the large-batch models achieve lower training losses. The result separates fitting the training data more closely from performing better on held-out data, supporting a beneficial role for stochastic gradient noise.

The paper also examines how the best learning-rate schedule changes as the available epoch budget increases. It provides a theoretical account using a stochastic differential equation view of SGD dynamics, linking the empirical observations to an analysis of noisy optimization. The conclusion is that gradient noise can enhance generalization, rather than that smaller batches are invariably superior for every model or training setup.
icml-2020-on-the-generalization-benefit-.tldr: Carefully tuned experiments show that stochastic gradient noise can improve test performance even when very large batches achieve lower training loss.

paragraphs: An optimizer's performance depends strongly on its hyperparameter settings. This paper argues that comparing optimizers only after finding nearly ideal settings can give practitioners an incomplete picture. Those settings may require a costly search, so the performance eventually achieved does not by itself capture how practical an optimizer is to use.

The authors propose accounting for the computational expense of automatic hyperparameter tuning when assessing optimizers. The relevant question includes how readily a search procedure finds good configurations. This places the cost of discovering effective settings alongside the quality of the resulting training run, making the comparison more closely reflect a practitioner working within a limited computational budget.

They evaluate a range of optimizers across an extensive collection of standard datasets and architectures. Their results indicate that Adam is the most practical option in those comparisons, especially when budgets are small. This is an empirical conclusion about optimizer performance when tuning cost is included. The broader methodological contribution is a criterion for benchmarking: strong results under carefully chosen settings should be assessed together with the effort needed to obtain those settings.
icml-2020-optimizer-benchmarking-needs-t.tldr: Optimizer comparisons should include hyperparameter search costs, with the paper's experiments favoring Adam especially under small budgets.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can require many interactions, making adaptation of a pretrained policy attractive. This paper focuses on adapting to unseen environments. It identifies a difficulty with approaches that sample target environments during pretraining: a new environment outside that sampled distribution can be challenging. The proposed approach instead introduces model-based mechanisms for online adaptation.

The mechanisms combine ideas from no-regret online learning and adaptive control. The authors prove that the approach learns policies in the target environment that can quickly recover trajectories from the source environment. They also establish a convergence rate in general settings. This gives the adaptation process a theoretical connection to recovering previously learned behavior under changed conditions.

Experiments examine a diverse set of continuous-control tasks. The approach achieves the performance of state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially fewer samples. The practical significance is that an existing policy can be adapted with fewer new interactions in the evaluated tasks. The theoretical and empirical contributions support efficient transfer through online model-based adaptation, rather than requiring all relevant target environments to have been represented during pretraining.
icml-2020-provably-efficient-model-based.tldr: Model-based online adaptation combines learning and control principles to recover source behavior and match leading control methods with fewer samples.

paragraphs: This paper reformulates molecular design as reinforcement learning in three-dimensional Cartesian coordinates. The authors identify a restriction of existing graph-based approaches: ignoring atoms' spatial locations limits the molecules they can construct and leads to heuristic rewards. Including coordinates extends the class of molecules the agent can build and makes spatial configuration part of the design problem.

The reward is based directly on fundamental physical properties, such as energy, estimated using fast quantum-chemical methods. This connects the learning signal to physical characteristics of the proposed structures. The authors also introduce MolGym, an environment containing several challenging molecular design tasks and baselines intended to support progress toward designing molecules from scratch.

Their agent operates in a state-action space that is invariant to translation and rotation. Moving or rotating the overall configuration therefore does not change that representation of the problem. Experiments show that the agent can efficiently learn the included tasks from scratch. The findings demonstrate a workable route to spatially explicit, physically guided molecular construction, with the physical rewards supplied through quantum-chemical approximations.
icml-2020-reinforcement-learning-for-mol.tldr: MolGym enables reinforcement learning to construct molecules in 3D using rewards derived from approximate quantum-chemical properties.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning uses penalties to balance reward against constraints, but the learning process can oscillate or overshoot. Those dynamics can produce constraint violations during training. This paper approaches the problem through control theory, interpreting the traditional update of a Lagrange multiplier as integral control and asking how to make that update more responsive.

The authors add proportional and derivative control terms using information from the constraint function. These additions introduce damping and predictive behavior into the multiplier update. The resulting PID Lagrangian method aims to improve how training responds to constraint behavior over time. The focus is therefore on the dynamics of enforcement during learning, not merely the final optimization objective.

Applied to deep reinforcement learning, the method achieves a reported new state of the art on Safety Gym. The authors also introduce invariance to the relative numerical scales of reward and cost to make controller tuning easier. Extensive experiments show improved performance and robustness to hyperparameter choices. These gains come with algorithms described as nearly as simple to derive and implement as the traditional Lagrangian approach.
icml-2020-responsive-safety-in-reinforce.tldr: PID-style multiplier updates improve constrained reinforcement learning dynamics and tuning robustness, with strong results on Safety Gym.

paragraphs: A relationship that predicts labels during training can become unreliable when the data distribution changes. This paper focuses on unmeasured variables, including confounders, that can cause such reversals. Its approach uses human causal knowledge to supplement training examples with a potential hidden variable, making that missing context part of the learning framework.

The annotation need not be a directly measured attribute: the authors describe adding a plausible unmeasured factor to an example. With these annotations, they formulate the problem as covariate shift and introduce UV-DRO, a distributionally robust optimization objective over unmeasured variables. The objective controls worst-case loss over possible test-time shifts represented in that formulation.

Experiments examine digit recognition with rotation as a confounder and analysis of NYPD Police Stops with location as a confounder. The authors report improvements of 5–10% and 1.5–5%, respectively. These results support the usefulness of combining human-supplied causal context with robust optimization in the evaluated settings. The framework gives such annotations a concrete role in preparing models for changing correlations, rather than treating all training associations as equally dependable.
icml-2020-robustness-to-spurious-correla.tldr: Human annotations of plausible hidden variables support a robust optimization objective that improves performance under confounded distribution shifts.

paragraphs: A robustness certificate specifies a distance within which input changes cannot alter a classifier's output. Computing exact certificates for neural networks is generally difficult because it involves non-convex optimization. This paper develops an efficient approach for networks with differentiable activation functions by using information about their curvature, captured through the Hessian.

The first result is conditional: if the Hessian's eigenvalues are bounded locally or globally, an L2 robustness certificate can be computed efficiently through convex optimization. The second contribution provides an efficiently computable, differentiable upper bound on deep-network curvature. Together, these results yield the proposed Curvature-based Robustness Certificate, or CRC.

The authors also use the curvature bound as a training regularizer, producing Curvature-based Robust Training, or CRT. This connects the quantity used for certification with a mechanism for improving certified robustness during learning. Numerical results show significantly higher certified robust accuracy than training based on interval-bound propagation. The guarantees concern perturbations smaller than the certificate value, and the method's stated setting requires differentiable activations and the relevant curvature bounds.
icml-2020-second-order-provable-defenses.tldr: Curvature bounds enable efficient L2 robustness certificates and a training regularizer that improves certified robust accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Large training batches can benefit generative adversarial networks, but processing them is expensive in time and memory. Small-GAN seeks some of those benefits through smaller selected batches. Its central idea is coreset selection: draw a large collection of candidates, then compress it into a subset for training. This changes how batches are formed.

For generated samples, the method draws a large batch from the prior and applies coreset selection. For real images, it first caches Inception activations for every training image and randomly projects those features into a smaller space. During training, coreset selection operates on the projected embeddings, using those representations to choose the real-image batch.

Experiments show substantial reductions in training time and memory use for modern GAN variants. On a synthetic dataset, the method also reduces the fraction of dropped modes, indicating better coverage of that dataset's different modes. The authors further report a new state of the art in anomaly detection using GANs. These findings support careful batch selection as a practical way to improve both resource use and aspects of model performance.
icml-2020-small-gan-speeding-up-gan-trai.tldr: Small-GAN selects compact coresets from larger candidate batches, reducing training costs and improving reported mode coverage and anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms usually balance exploiting current knowledge against deliberately exploring alternatives. This paper studies a setting where useful exploration can arise implicitly. It assumes adversarial contexts are perturbed by Gaussian noise and that the unknown linear parameter has structure, such as sparsity, group sparsity, or low rank. The perturbation assumption is central to the analysis.

The authors propose simple greedy algorithms for both a shared-parameter setting and a setting with different parameters for different contexts. They develop a unified regret analysis that accommodates an assumed parameter structure. The bounds depend on geometric quantities, including Gaussian widths, which express how the structure enters the learning guarantee.

The improved analysis also gives sharper regret bounds for the unstructured case than earlier work. The main conclusion is that a greedy algorithm can work in this smoothed setting because the perturbed contexts supply implicit exploration. This explains why deliberate exploration need not always be essential under the stated conditions. It does not remove the role of exploration in arbitrary contexts; the result specifically depends on the analyzed smoothed model.
icml-2020-structured-linear-contextual-b.tldr: Under Gaussian-perturbed contexts, greedy structured linear bandits benefit from implicit exploration and admit unified geometric regret bounds.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning commonly begins with tasks that people have already defined and labeled. This paper asks how a system could instead infer task concepts from basic input-output examples. When examples from several tasks are mixed without task identifiers, the combined mapping becomes confusing because the system must determine how the examples relate to different underlying tasks.

The authors introduce Confusing Supervised Learning, or CSL, to extract task concepts by differentiating among those mixed examples. They provide a theoretical feasibility result for the framework and design an iterative algorithm that distinguishes tasks. The proposed learning problem therefore includes discovering the task distinctions, rather than assuming those distinctions have been supplied before training.

Experiments cover multi-function regression and multi-task recognition. The authors describe their results as showing that CSL can achieve human-like task understanding without task labels in those problems. The input-output supervision remains available; what is absent is the annotation identifying each example's task. The findings support learning useful task distinctions from mixed supervised data, with the demonstrated scope tied to the regression and recognition settings evaluated.
icml-2020-task-understanding-from-confus.tldr: Confusing Supervised Learning infers task distinctions from mixed input-output examples without explicit task labels.

paragraphs: Attribution methods highlight image regions intended to explain a neural network's prediction. This paper examines methods that propagate custom relevance scores backward through the network using modified backpropagation rules. The central question is whether those explanations remain sensitive to the learned model, especially the parameters in its later layers.

The authors study Deep Taylor Decomposition, Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, Excitation Backpropagation, PatternAttribution, DeepLIFT, Deconv, RectGrad, and Guided Backpropagation. Empirically, they find that all examined methods except DeepLIFT produce explanations independent of later-layer parameters. They provide theoretical insights into this behavior and analyze why DeepLIFT avoids the particular limitation they identify.

To measure how later-layer information is ignored, the paper introduces cosine similarity convergence, or CSC. The metric complements the theoretical analysis with an empirical assessment of information loss in the explanation process. The contribution is a framework for evaluating the faithfulness of modified backpropagation methods. DeepLIFT's exception concerns the identified failure mode; the abstract does not present it as proof that every explanation it produces is fully faithful.
icml-2020-when-explanations-lie-why-many.tldr: Many examined modified-backpropagation explanations empirically ignore later-layer parameters, with DeepLIFT avoiding this identified failure mode.

paragraphs: A single network can solve several vision tasks at once, potentially reducing the computation needed at inference time. However, sharing a network can also hurt overall performance when task objectives compete. This paper studies which tasks cooperate and which interfere, treating the choice of task grouping as a central part of building an efficient multi-task system.

The authors examine task cooperation and competition across several learning settings. They then propose a framework that assigns tasks to a small number of networks. Cooperating tasks share a network, while competing tasks are assigned to different networks. This creates intermediate arrangements between one network handling every task and a separate network for each task.

The framework offers a tradeoff between inference time and accuracy. The authors report that it can achieve higher accuracy with less inference time than both a single large multi-task network and a collection of single-task networks. The result shows that selective sharing can improve both objectives in the studied settings. The useful design decision is therefore not only how much to share, but which tasks should share their computation.
icml-2020-which-tasks-should-be-learned-.tldr: Grouping cooperating tasks into shared networks can improve both accuracy and inference time compared with fully shared or fully separate models.
